Issued at 100 PM CDT Fri Oct 23 2026

This Afternoon - Sunday: Mostly Dry, Low Precipitation Potential

Primarily dry conditions continue throughout the rest of this 
afternoon and through much of the weekend as upper level ridging
slowly shifts eastward. However, an area of shortwave energy 
reflected at 700-500hPa currently over the north-central 
Iowa/south- central Minnesota is expected to continue lifting 
northward along the western side of the ridge this afternoon 
into the evening. 700- 500hPa positive vorticity advection and 
700hPa frontogenesis associated with this shortwave trough 
combined with some modest mid to upper level moisture advection 
may result in scattered sprinkles to light showers this 
afternoon. Not expecting much in the way of impacts, if we even 
see rain at the surface at all, as dry air below 10kft depicted 
in RRFS/RAP/HRRR soundings acts to evaporate the bulk of any 
rain as it falls. However, there have been observations of light
rain associated with these forcings upstream so a few hundreths
of rain does not appear unreasonable.

While the shortwave trough continues working its way across our
area tonight, a strong upper level low moves eastward across 
Canada, dragging a cold front into the Upper Midwest by late 
Saturday. This feature stalls out across Minnesota into northern
Wisconsin as it becomes separated from the upper level support,
remaining somewhere north of I-90 into Sunday. Weak moisture 
advects along this boundary under southerly flow as various 
shortwave troughs eject northward from a cutoff low across the 
Desert Southwest, promoting some low chances for light rain late
Saturday through Sunday (10-20%). 

Next Week: Greater Precipitation Potential, Trending Cooler

The stalled cold front begins to slowly sag southward late
Sunday into early next week, allowing cooler air to filter into
the region. There's still some uncertainty regarding what
temperatures will ultimately be due to variations in how far
south the boundary makes it and the influence from potential
rainfall, but the 23.13z NBM mean suggests highs top out in the
upper 50s to low 60s.

Late Sunday into Monday, the cutoff low over the Desert 
Southwest begins to move northward, prompting a surface low to 
develop across the Great Plains. The various ensemble suites 
(GEFS/EPS/GEPS) appear to be in a bit better agreement about how
these features evolve early next week though there is still 
some variation regarding the track of these features.

Currently, the ECMWF/Canadian suites suggest these features 
take a more northern trajectory resulting in lower rainfall 
amounts across our area whereas the GFS takes a more southerly 
track, bringing greater rainfall amounts to the Mississippi 
River Valley. Tending towards an ECMWF/Canadian solution, so 
thinking that our western and northern counties will be the ones
to see the bulk of any precipitation. Around half of the 23.00z
LREF members favor this solution (40-50%), which is in 
agreement with the 23.13z NBM that suggests 40-70% probabilities
for rainfall for these counties. Regardless, not expecting a 
washout by any means. Deterministic amounts range from 0.25-0.5 
inches in the GFS/AIGFS and Euro/AIFS with some potential for 
amounts greater than 0.5 inches per the NBM, around 20-40%. 
However, given the favored northern track, the greatest 
potential for amounts higher than 0.5 inches exist across 
central into east-central Minnesota, out of our area. 

Midweek, there's some modest agreement within the 23.00z LREF 
membership that a shortwave trough moves across the northern 
United States, phasing with a longwave trough across Canada. A 
surface low pressure system looks to develop across the Midwest 
in response to these features bringing some additional rainfall 
potential, currently a 20-40% chance per the 23.13z NBM, and 
possibly some breezy winds before high pressure and dry 
conditions return by late next week.
